metricNotes.coupling: Measures inbound coupling (fan-in) only. A zone with coupling: 0 (e.g. routes) means no other zone imports from it — it does NOT mean the zone has no outbound dependencies. Routes has the highest outbound import count (depends on hooks, components) but this is expected for a leaf layer. Do not interpret low inbound coupling as low overall coupling for leaf zones.
metricNotes.cohesion: Infrastructure zones (build-infrastructure, project-infrastructure) report cohesion: 0 because their files are standalone config artifacts with no mutual imports. This is structurally normal — config files are not modules that import each other — and does not indicate logical fragmentation. A cohesion score of 0 in these zones should not be treated as a warning.
metricNotes.zoneSize: game-engine contains ~45% of project files but reports cohesion 0.87 and coupling 0.13 — the high file count reflects a genuinely interconnected domain (types, traversal, scoring, biome theming, hooks, rendering components) rather than an over-broad grouping. The zone's internal cohesion exceeds 2x the warning threshold (0.4), confirming it is a natural domain boundary. Route files (play.tsx, worlds.tsx) are overridden out of this zone since they are UI composition layers, not engine logic.
metricNotes.bidirectionalCoupling: The original bidirectional coupling between game-engine and gameplay-ui (2+9 crossings) has been resolved to unidirectional flow. The 2 reverse crossings (engine → gameplay-ui) were caused by play.tsx being classified in game-engine while importing MobileInventory/TileInventory from gameplay-ui — resolved by the play.tsx zone override. TilePreview.tsx was reclassified from game-engine to gameplay-ui because its only consumers (MobileInventory, TileInventory) are in gameplay-ui; its dependency on engine/index.ts follows the correct DAG direction (gameplay-ui → game-engine). The remaining crossings (gameplay-ui → game-engine) represent the expected unidirectional data flow: UI components consuming engine types, constants, and hooks through the barrel.
metricNotes.gameplayUiCoupling: gameplay-ui reports coupling 0.58 from 9 imports targeting game-engine. This is structurally expected: gameplay-ui is a leaf UI-composition zone whose sole purpose is to render engine state. The 9 imports break down as: 5 type/constant imports from the engine barrel (TileType, TILE_TYPE_DEFS, WorldData, LevelData, SVG_WIDTH/SVG_HEIGHT), 2 TilePreview component imports, and 2 hook imports (useWorldSession, useRainbowEasterEgg). All follow the correct DAG direction (UI → engine). The coupling score is below the warning threshold and the risk level is healthy. Reducing these imports would require either duplicating engine types in the UI layer or adding an unnecessary abstraction layer.
metricNotes.worldNavigationSeparation: world-navigation originally contained both route handlers (worlds.tsx, home.tsx) and display components (RainbowArc.tsx, WorldGrid.tsx), conflating routing and presentation responsibilities. RainbowArc.tsx and WorldGrid.tsx are overridden to world-selection-ui because they are presentation components consumed exclusively by worlds.tsx — this follows the same pattern as gameplay-ui (play.tsx + TilePreview.tsx). world-navigation now contains only route handlers (home.tsx), cleanly separating routing from presentation.
metricNotes.zoneBoundariesTestScope: zone-boundaries.test.ts guards the entire 4-layer architecture DAG (engine → hooks → components → routes), making its conceptual scope global rather than zone-specific. It is classified in build-infrastructure because it is the runtime verification counterpart to eslint.config.ts — the static rule definition it validates. Both files form a cohesive pair: one defines the enforcement rules, the other proves they are correctly wired. This is not a misclassification; architecture enforcement tooling belongs with the build infrastructure that implements it.
metricNotes.worldSelectionUiCouplingConcentration: Within world-selection-ui, worlds.tsx accounts for 3 of 4 cross-zone imports (all into game-engine via the hooks barrel), while RainbowArc.tsx has zero and WorldGrid.tsx has 1 (engine types). This concentration is structurally correct: worlds.tsx is the composition root that mounts SaveProvider, consumes hooks (useWorldSession, useRainbowEasterEgg), and passes data down to presentation components via props. RainbowArc.tsx and WorldGrid.tsx having zero or minimal engine imports is the desired outcome — it means they are pure presentation components receiving data through props rather than reaching into the engine directly. The zone's coupling score should not be interpreted as evenly distributed; the concentration in the composition root is the expected pattern for a route handler orchestrating a provider + hook + component tree.
